bibl.title: Measuring vaccine hesitancy: The development of a survey tool

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: HOW TO MEASURE `vaccine hesitancy` - a construct defined by the same working group, in the adjacent article of the same journal supplement, three months earlier
span.quote: “Vaccine hesitancy refers to a delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite availability of vaccination services. Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place, and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence”

span.label: what to ask, of whom, so that the scale and nature of hesitancy can be compared across countries - and how to keep the answer from counting refusal, or access failure, as hesitancy
span.quote: Tools are needed to assess the scope and scale of hesitancy issues by vaccine and setting. Ideally, a common survey tool that can be used globally would allow comparability across countries.

span.label: a compendium of survey questions in three forms - closed, Likert and open-ended - mapped onto the Determinants Matrix, plus two indicators piloted in the WHO-UNICEF Joint Reporting Form
span.quote: The Working Group developed a compendium of three different types of survey questions (See Appendices): Core Closed Questions (Appendix A); Likert Scale Questions (Appendix B); and a set of Open Ended Questions (Appendix C). Some were derived from previously validated questionnaires, albeit in high-income countries only, some came from experts in the field, and others are newly proposed.

span.label: method
span.quote: The Working Group developed a compendium of three different types of survey questions (See Appendices): Core Closed Questions (Appendix A); Likert Scale Questions (Appendix B); and a set of Open Ended Questions (Appendix C). Some were derived from previously validated questionnaires, albeit in high-income countries only, some came from experts in the field, and others are newly proposed.

span.label: hesitancy as a SUB-GROUP property rather than a population-wide one, so that the measurement has to answer WHO, WHAT and WHERE separately
span.quote: Given that vaccine hesitancy is specific to sub-groups within populations and is rarely population-wide, it is important to first understand _who_ is hesitant about vaccination, _what_ their concerns are – i.e. which of the various possible reasons outlined above are driving their hesitancy, and _where_ the hesitant individuals are located, i.e. in which geographic, socio-cultural or political context that may be contributing to the hesitancy.

span.label: items harvested from a systematic review by two keyword searches, re-screening 2,933 articles, then supplemented by expert contribution and newly written questions; two indicators pilot-tested through national Joint Reporting Forms
span.term: items harvested from a systematic review by two keyword searches, re-screening 2,933 articles, then supplemented by expert contribution and newly written questions; two indicators pilot-tested through national Joint Reporting Forms
span.quote: A selection of articles ( _n_ = 2933) were re-screened for this purpose. Keyword searches included: **Search 1**: ‘Survey’ and any one of ‘accept/barrier/refus/trust/missed/delay/confidence/partial/unsure/timeliness/hesitan’ **Search 2**: ‘Scale/Index/measurement/instrument/Questionnaire’ and any one of ‘Trust/Confidence/Hesitan’ These keywords were chosen to identify either complete surveys or survey items that reflect the concern of vaccine hesitancy.

span.label: the survey is built to separate three things a raw uptake figure cannot: REFUSAL, ACCESS FAILURE, and HESITANCY. `Counting only vaccine refusers will not capture hesitancy`, and the reasons for being unvaccinated must be assessed to tackle hesitancy `AS DISTINCT FROM ACCESS ISSUES`
span.quote: When countries use questions presented in this paper to monitor hesitancy, several points must be considered in question selection: (1) Refusal is not the same as hesitancy, i.e. counting only vaccine refusers will not capture hesitancy

span.label: and it is built to be VACCINE-SPECIFIC, because the construct is: hesitancy `may be specific to one or some, but not all, vaccines`, so a survey answer must not be generalised across vaccines unless the question said so
span.quote: (3) Vaccine hesitancy may be specific to one or some, but not all, vaccines, so interpretation of surveys should not generalize findings to all vaccines unless that is stated in the survey response.

span.label: THE DEFINITION IS RESTATED IN A NARROWER FORM THAN ITS OWN SOURCE PAPER USES. macdonald2015 writes `delay in acceptance or refusal of VACCINATION despite availability of VACCINATION SERVICES`; this paper's Discussion writes `delay in acceptance or refusal of VACCINES despite availability of VACCINE SERVICES`. macdonald2015 spent a paragraph choosing the narrower NAME while keeping the broader SENSE, and the breadth lived in exactly those two words
span.quote: Vaccine hesitancy is defined as _delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccine services_

span.label: and the Introduction's block quotation differs from the source too, in two places: `A delay` for `delay`, and `time, place, and vaccines` for `time, place and vaccines`. Small, and they establish that THE DEFINITION IS BEING RE-TYPED RATHER THAN COPIED - which is how the third version becomes possible
span.quote: “Vaccine hesitancy refers to a delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite availability of vaccination services. Vaccine hesitancy is complex and context specific, varying across time, place, and vaccines. It is influenced by factors such as complacency, convenience and confidence”

span.label: THE FIRST INSTRUMENT MEASURED SOMETHING ELSE ON PURPOSE: the 2012 pilot focused on vaccine confidence `RATHER THAN on the broader issues driving vaccine hesitancy`, `IN ORDER TO BE IN HARMONY WITH THE GLOBAL VACCINE ACTION PLAN INDICATORS`. The instrument was aligned to a programme's reporting framework before it was aligned to the construct
span.quote: In the 2012 JRF pilot test, the focus was on vaccine confidence, rather than on the broader issues driving vaccine hesitancy, in order to be in harmony with the Global Vaccine Action Plan indicators.

span.label: the pilot it reports on had a 14% response rate - 13 of 94 countries - and the paper calls it `SUB-OPTIMAL` in its own first results sentence
span.quote: The response rate to the first JRF pilot in 2012 was sub-optimal with only 14% (13/94) of countries completing the questions. The analysis revealed that 19% of all participating countries had done an assessment of the level of confidence in their country, indicating that vaccine confidence was an issue of concern in their country.

span.label: THE QUESTIONS ARE LARGELY UNVALIDATED AND THE PAPER SAYS SO THREE TIMES: `few have been validated`; `most are predominately designed for HIGH-INCOME SETTINGS`; and the questions `DO NOT ADDRESS ALL THE DETERMINANTS in the Vaccine Hesitancy Matrix`
span.quote: As the term “vaccine hesitancy” is relatively new, the availability of existing survey questions is limited. Most are predominately designed for high-income settings, and few have been validated. Furthermore, the questions identified do not address all the determinants in the Vaccine Hesitancy Matrix and additional questions will need to be developed and validated.

span.label: and SAGE's own final report is quoted saying the compendium has been `ASSESSED AND VALIDATED ONLY IN SOME HIGH-INCOME COUNTRIES OR NOT AT ALL` - a validation warning carried inside the paper that ships the instrument
span.quote: In the final report on the work on vaccine hesitancy, SAGE “encouraged validation of the developed compendium of survey questions on vaccine hesitancy, which have been assessed and validated only in some high-income countries or not at all.

span.label: the items are of MIXED PROVENANCE and it is declared: some `derived from previously validated questionnaires, ALBEIT IN HIGH-INCOME COUNTRIES ONLY`, some from experts, and `others are NEWLY PROPOSED`. Three evidential grades in one compendium, distinguishable nowhere in the instrument itself
span.quote: The Working Group developed a compendium of three different types of survey questions (See Appendices): Core Closed Questions (Appendix A); Likert Scale Questions (Appendix B); and a set of Open Ended Questions (Appendix C). Some were derived from previously validated questionnaires, albeit in high-income countries only, some came from experts in the field, and others are newly proposed.

span.label: and the construct is declared UNSTABLE IN TIME, which limits any single measurement: `a survey which reveals little hesitancy this year MAY HAVE A DIFFERENT RESULT NEXT YEAR`
span.quote: Given the dynamic and changing nature of vaccine hesitancy, the importance of ongoing monitoring cannot be overstated. A survey which reveals little hesitancy this year may have a different result next year.

span.label: the funding disclosure is IDENTICAL to its companion paper's, and lands on the same word: the group monitoring `public confidence in Immunization Programs` took Novartis research funding and GSK meeting funding, and the first author consulted for GSK ON VACCINE CONFIDENCE
span.quote: The LSHTM research group “Project to monitor public confidence in Immunization Programs” has received research funding from Novartis as well as funding from GSK to host a meeting on vaccine confidence. Heidi Larson has done consulting on vaccine confidence with GSK.

span.label: whether the instrument counts refusal, or access failure, as hesitancy
span.note: eliminates: both confounds AT THE LEVEL OF INSTRUCTION - the paper states that refusal is not hesitancy and that hesitancy must be assessed as distinct from access - but no item, scoring rule or threshold is given that would separate them in a returned survey · outcome: partial
span.quote: When countries use questions presented in this paper to monitor hesitancy, several points must be considered in question selection: (1) Refusal is not the same as hesitancy, i.e. counting only vaccine refusers will not capture hesitancy

span.label: whether the questions have been validated
span.note: eliminates: nothing, declared three times over: `few have been validated`, `most are predominately designed for high-income settings`, and SAGE's own report says they are validated `ONLY IN SOME HIGH-INCOME COUNTRIES OR NOT AT ALL` · outcome: failed
span.quote: As the term “vaccine hesitancy” is relatively new, the availability of existing survey questions is limited. Most are predominately designed for high-income settings, and few have been validated. Furthermore, the questions identified do not address all the determinants in the Vaccine Hesitancy Matrix and additional questions will need to be developed and validated.

span.label: whether the item pool covers the construct it is mapped onto
span.note: eliminates: nothing - the questions `do not address all the determinants in the Vaccine Hesitancy Matrix`, and the remedy offered is that more `will need to be developed and validated` · outcome: failed
span.quote: As the term “vaccine hesitancy” is relatively new, the availability of existing survey questions is limited. Most are predominately designed for high-income settings, and few have been validated. Furthermore, the questions identified do not address all the determinants in the Vaccine Hesitancy Matrix and additional questions will need to be developed and validated.

span.label: the two JRF indicators were pilot-tested across the Americas, Europe and East, South and Central Africa, in four languages, before being proposed
span.note: eliminates: single-region wording effects as an explanation of the responses - the paper says the spread `allowed for input from a broad range of high, middle and low-income countries` · outcome: partial
span.quote: Modifications to the 2013 JRF included refining the indicators to encompass the wider scope of vaccine hesitancy reasons going beyond confidence to also include convenience and complacency, and to link with the revised Working Group definition of vaccine hesitancy.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vaccine.2015.04.037.
